name: Reference guides
title: Several sources, one place to find an answer.
description: Combine chapters, slides and notes into a guide organized around the questions people need answered. Useful for clinical differentials, technical handbooks and operating procedures.
brief: Create a practical reference guide from these sources. Organize it around the questions the reader needs to answer. Explain the complete answer, including conditions, exceptions and findings that distinguish similar cases. Combine questions only when they ask the same thing. Explain disagreements between sources and identify which source applies. Use comparison tables where helpful, cite supporting passages and state what you left out.
inputs: Add chapters, slides or notes. Mark each file as a factual source, supporting context, an older version or a style example.
stages: Collect ideas and supporting passages. Keep slide text, tables and speaker notes together.
Combine questions that ask the same thing. Keep separate cases when their conditions change the answer.
Write each section using the outline and its supporting sources.
Check sections against the sources, revise flagged passages, and save HTML, Markdown or PDF.
decision: Organizing the questions first gives each section a clear purpose and makes missing answers easier to spot.
context: Writers receive the outline, their assigned material and the supporting passages they need.
delivery: HTML, PDF and Markdown, with source citations.
revision: Request a change to one section. Its writer and reviewer run again; unchanged requests reuse saved results. Replan when the sources or goal change.

name: Podcasts
title: Turn your sources into an audio lesson.
description: Create a script with a clear sequence, explanations, examples and recall questions. Connect a speech service to create audio.
brief: Write an educational podcast script for a practitioner listening during a commute. Arrange the material in a clear order with natural section breaks. Explain unfamiliar terms, mechanisms, quantities and exceptions. Use examples and brief recall questions. Keep terminology consistent, label speakers and write clear transitions between sections.
inputs: Add your sources and describe who will listen and what they should learn. Connect a speech service in the local app if you want audio.
stages: Choose the order and identify what each section needs to explain.
Draft the sections, check them against the sources and revise any problems.
Convert the finished script to audio, one section at a time.
decision: A shared outline keeps the sections on topic. Exact callbacks to an earlier section’s wording require a custom workflow that waits for that section.
context: Writers receive the lesson outline, their assigned material and relevant earlier ideas.
delivery: Podcast script, with optional WAV audio.
revision: Revise and check the affected section. Regenerate its audio while reusing unchanged recordings.

name: Practice exams
title: Create questions with a separate answer key.
description: Build cases and short-answer questions with separate candidate sheets and marking guides. A model attempts each question without seeing the key, then another call checks the answer.
brief: Create a short-answer practice exam for practitioners using these sources. Build cases around meaningful decisions, revealing new information in stages. State what each question asks and any answer limit. Keep expected answers, marks, explanations and acceptable alternatives in a separate answer key. Include questions that ask candidates to apply knowledge, interpret findings and reconsider an earlier decision. Preserve source conditions and numerical criteria.
inputs: Add factual sources and supporting material. Mark example questions as style examples. Questions reserved for testing are excluded from generation.
stages: Identify the knowledge and decisions the questions should test.
Create clear prompts, expected answers and marking guidance.
A model answers using only the information available to the candidate. A separate review checks the answer against the key.
Save the question sheet and answer key separately. Include any unresolved issues in the review.
decision: Trying each question without the key helps reveal ambiguity, missing information and answers that do not match the marking guide.
context: Writers see the outline and sources. The test solver sees only the question and any required earlier prompts. A separate reviewer checks its answer against the key.
delivery: Candidate and examiner files, plus review findings.
revision: Edit the affected section and run the assessment checks again. Questions that depend on revised earlier information receive a new candidate context.
